title: Calling Out From the Depths
overview: Someone in deep trouble begs God to listen, trusts that God forgives rather than keeping score, waits for help like a guard waiting for dawn, and then urges the whole nation of Israel to hope in the same way.

parts.label: A cry from the bottom (vv. 1-2)
parts.note: "The depths" is an old picture of deep, overwhelming water, standing for crushing trouble or near despair. The writer never says what the trouble is and simply pleads with God to hear.

parts.label: No one survives a strict record (vv. 3-4)
parts.note: If God kept a running list of every wrong, no one could "stand," probably picturing an accused person standing upright in court, but God forgives instead. The verse links that forgiveness to reverence without spelling out why, and one common reading is that people can only serve a God who will not throw them out for every fault.

parts.label: Waiting like a night watchman (vv. 5-6)
parts.note: Guards on a city wall sat through the dark, sure that morning would come and longing for it, and the repeated line stresses how long and eager this waiting is. The writer's hope rests on "his word," usually understood as what God has promised.

parts.label: Hope for the whole people (vv. 7-8)
parts.note: The psalm widens from one person to Israel, pointing to God's loyal, steady love and to "redemption," meaning being bought back or set free, here from sin itself and not just from enemies. Christians have read this promise in light of Jesus, who in the New Testament is said to save his people from their sins.

think: Is it easier for you to let go of other people's wrongs, or to believe your own could be let go?
